opus-5.5.text:
I think our core advantage really comes down to three things working together.

The first is fidelity at the level that actually matters for robot learning. A lot of people think of Real2Sim as just reconstructing what a scene looks like, getting nice visuals with something like Gaussian splatting or NeRF. But for a robot, appearance is only part of the story. What really determines whether a policy transfers back to the real world is geometry that's accurate enough for contact, and physical properties: mass, friction, articulation, how a drawer slides, how a cloth deforms. We've put a lot of effort into recovering those physical attributes, not just the surface, so the simulated object behaves the way the real one does when a gripper touches it.

The second is scale and automation. If reconstructing one kitchen takes an engineer a week of manual tuning, that's a demo, not infrastructure. What we've tried to build is a pipeline where you can capture a real environment with fairly ordinary hardware, like a phone or a handheld scanner, and turn it into a simulation-ready, interactive asset with very little human intervention. Once that's true, you can go from tens of scenes to thousands, and that diversity is what gives generalization.

The third, and I'd say the most important, is that we close the loop. We don't treat Real2Sim as a one-way conversion. We train policies in the reconstructed environments, deploy them on real robots, look at where they fail, and use that gap to correct the simulation, whether it's the physics parameters or the rendering. Over time the sim-to-real gap gets smaller in a measurable way rather than us just hoping it's small.

So if I had to sum it up: other teams may be very strong on visual reconstruction, or on simulators, or on policy learning. Our advantage is connecting all three into one system, where real-world data becomes training environments at scale, and the real world keeps validating and calibrating those environments. In embodied intelligence, data is the bottleneck, and I see Real2Sim as one of the most practical ways to multiply limited real-world data into something much larger and still trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response says manual scene reconstruction limits scale, but does not state that high per-object physical-parameter acquisition costs prevent high-quality simulation from scaling.

r002.rationale: It contrasts visual scene reconstruction with recovering physical attributes such as mass, friction, and articulation so simulated objects behave like real ones.

r003.rationale: It mentions ordinary capture hardware and gripper contact, but does not describe inferring physical parameters from both equipment data and robot-object interactions.

r004.rationale: It mentions scaling to thousands of diverse scenes, but not generalizing acquired physical parameters across assets and scenes according to distributions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core advantage really comes down to two things: data and the pipeline that turns that data into something a simulator can actually use.

On the data side, most people doing simulation start from assets that were hand-built or scanned once, and they look fine but they're static. They don't carry the messiness of the real world: how a cloth drapes differently depending on humidity, how a door hinge has a bit of friction that changes over time, how lighting bounces off a surface that's slightly worn. What we focus on is capturing those physical properties directly from real scenes, not just geometry and texture, but things like material response, contact dynamics, how objects deform under force. That's the part most reconstruction pipelines throw away, and it's exactly what a robot needs if the policy it learns in sim is going to survive contact with the real world.

The second thing is closing the loop. Real2Sim isn't a one-shot process for us. You capture, you build the digital twin, you run the policy, and then you compare what happened in sim to what the real robot did. Where they diverge, that gap tells you what your simulation got wrong, and you go back and refine the physical parameters. So over time the simulator becomes calibrated against reality rather than being a rough approximation of it. That iterative tightening is where I think we're genuinely ahead, because it compounds. Every real-world rollout makes the sim better, and a better sim means the next batch of synthetic data is more trustworthy.

And honestly, the reason this matters is scale. Real robot data is expensive and slow to collect. If you can get a simulator that's faithful enough that training in it transfers with minimal fine-tuning, you unlock orders of magnitude more data. The whole bet is that the bottleneck in embodied AI isn't model architecture, it's getting enough physically grounded experience, and Real2Sim is the most practical bridge to that.

r001.rationale: It says real-robot data is expensive and slow, but does not explain that acquiring physical parameters per object is costly or that this prevents high-quality simulation from scaling.

r002.rationale: It contrasts physical properties with geometry and texture, but does not distinguish physics-based Real2Sim reconstruction from vision-based reconstruction.

r003.rationale: It describes capturing physical properties and refining parameters through real-robot comparisons, but not automatically inferring them from physical-data collection equipment and robot-object interactions.

r004.rationale: It describes refining a digital twin against reality, but not generalizing acquired physical parameters across assets and scenes according to distributions.

astra-6.text:
I’d say my core advantage is thinking about the whole loop: what we capture from the physical world, how we represent it in simulation, and whether that simulation actually helps us solve the real-world task.

For me, Real2Sim isn’t just about making a scene look realistic. It’s about preserving the properties that matter for interaction—geometry, motion, contact, and physical behavior. A visually convincing model can still be a poor simulator if those properties are wrong.

So I focus on identifying what needs to be accurate, what we can simplify, and how to validate those choices against real observations. That connection between reconstruction and useful simulation is where I see my strongest contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say our core advantage is in connecting real-world observations to the physical properties a simulation needs. Capturing how something looks is one part of the problem, but we also need to understand how it moves, how it responds to contact, and how it interacts with its environment.

For me, Real2Sim is a loop: observe the real world, build a model, compare its behavior with reality, and refine it. The value comes from making that loop efficient and reliable, so the simulation becomes useful for testing and learning.

r001.rationale: It says the real-to-simulation loop should be efficient and reliable, but does not explain that costly per-object physical-parameter acquisition prevents high-quality simulation from scaling.
